title: Senior's toolkit: scanning, firewalls and SSH hardening
summary: Check what a host exposes, read the firewall that is really loaded, confirm the SSH settings in effect, and find attacks in the logs.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: scanning, firewalls and SSH hardening
steps.body: Security basics on a server are about facts, not intentions: what is actually reachable, which rules are actually loaded, which SSH settings are actually in effect. Scan only hosts you own or are allowed to test.

toolkit.what: Which ports answer from the outside, and which service and version is behind each. The attacker's first view of your host.
flags: skip the ping check (for hosts that drop ICMP)
toolkit.when: after every firewall change, run from outside the network

toolkit.what: The firewall rules the kernel really has loaded. nftables is the default on current Debian, Ubuntu and RHEL; `iptables` there often writes into nftables.
flags: show handles, to delete one rule
says `(nf_tables)` or `(legacy)`: which backend you are really editing

toolkit.what: The legacy view, still common on older hosts and in scripts. `-v` shows packet counters, so you can see which rule actually matches traffic.
flags: packet and byte counters per rule

toolkit.what: On Ubuntu hosts that use ufw: the allowed ports and the default policies, in plain words.
flags: rules plus default incoming and outgoing policy
rules with numbers, for `ufw delete N`
ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 22 proto tcp

toolkit.what: Prints the SSH server settings in effect after every include and default. The only reliable answer to "is password login really off?".
flags: test the config for errors before a reload

toolkit.what: SSH log for the last hour: failed passwords, invalid users and accepted keys. The unit is `ssh` on Debian and Ubuntu, `sshd` on RHEL and Fedora.
flags: only the messages, for piping into awk
toolkit.example: sudo journalctl -u ssh --since today --grep 'Failed password' -o cat | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

toolkit.what: Shows how many addresses the `sshd` jail has banned and which ones. Confirms brute-force protection is working.
flags: counts and banned IPs for that jail
lift a ban (a colleague locked out)

steps.prompt: Match each command to the question it answers.
pairs: which SSH settings are really in effect?
what does this host expose to the outside?
am I editing nftables or legacy iptables?
which addresses are banned for SSH brute force?
which rule is actually matching packets?

steps.prompt: You set `PasswordAuthentication no` at the end of `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` and reloaded, but an `nmap` script still reports that password login is offered. What do you run?
options: `sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication`, then look in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/` for an earlier file that sets it to `yes`
steps.explain: For most sshd options the first value read wins. Files in `sshd_config.d/` are included near the top of `sshd_config`, so a cloud image's `50-cloud-init.conf` with `yes` beats your line at the bottom. `sshd -T` shows the winner.

steps.prompt: You added an iptables rule to drop port 8080, `iptables -L` shows it, but `nmap` from outside still finds 8080 open. `iptables -V` says `(legacy)` and `nft list ruleset` shows a large ruleset with an accept for 8080. What is going on?
options: Two firewall backends are loaded; the traffic is accepted by the nftables rules you did not edit. Manage one backend only
steps.explain: Mixing `iptables-legacy` with nftables (for example from Docker or firewalld) is a classic trap. Pick the tool the distro uses, usually nft or its front end, and remove the other.

steps.prompt: Scan the 100 most common ports on a host that ignores ping, and identify the services.
steps.explain: `-Pn` treats the host as up without pinging it, `-sV` identifies the service on each open port. `-sn` would do the opposite: a ping sweep with no port scan.

steps.prompt: Turn off SSH password logins without locking yourself out.
lines: Confirm key login works in a second session: ssh -o PasswordAuthentication=no ops@web01
sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication   # confirm what is in effect

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: After any firewall or SSH change, prove it from the outside (`nmap`) and from the inside (`sshd -T`, `nft list ruleset`), and keep a second SSH session open until you have. Check the auth log weekly; a spike in failed logins is often the first sign that something is exposed.
